descripcion: At C1 a story is built for tension, not just sequence: an opening that withholds the point, a clearly marked turning point, and a closing line that generalises beyond the single event. The grammar (past tenses) is already known; what changes is the architecture of the telling.

filas: It's changed how I see the whole thing since.

ejemplos.texto: I never saw it coming, to be honest.
And then, out of nowhere, the whole plan fell apart.
It's changed how I approach things ever since.

notas: Starting with a date or a flat time marker is the single most common way a C1 story loses its listener in the first sentence.
The turning point needs a verbal signal (and then, out of nowhere, that's when) — without it, the shift gets lost in the flow.
A strong closing line draws a general lesson, not just a summary of what happened.

contraste.es: El español narra con más digresiones y subtramas incrustadas, y el punto de inflexión suele quedar implícito en el orden de los hechos más que marcado con una palabra explícita. Los hispanohablantes tienden a omitir el marcador verbal del giro (and then, out of nowhere), lo que en inglés hace que la historia pierda tensión.

errores: Starting with a date or plain time reference instead of creating curiosity.
Leaving the turning point unmarked, so it blends into the rest of the narration.
Ending the story flatly with no generalising closing line.

autochequeo: Does the story open with something other than a date?
Is the turning point clearly marked with a verbal signal?
Does the closing line generalise beyond the single event?
Are past simple, continuous and perfect correctly distributed?
Would a listener stay curious through the opening two sentences?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the dramaturgy of the story: opening, turning point, closing. Check whether all three are present and clearly signalled. Do not rewrite the text.
